record.paper_title: Phase-type distributions and representations: Some results and open problems for system theory
record.original_question: How is cyclicity in the directed graph of a phase-type representation related to the occurrence of non-real poles in the Laplace transform of the associated phase-type distribution? Characterize when cyclicity is compulsory, when a distribution with real poles can nevertheless have a natural or smaller cyclic representation, and whether cyclic representations can have smaller order than every acyclic representation of the same distribution.

evidence.quote: In some cases the cyclicity is compulsory, that is when the Laplace transform of the distribution has non-real poles.
But in some cases there may exist cyclic representations which may be of a smaller order than any acyclic one.
From this discussion it appears that the relation between the cyclicity of the representation and the existence of non-real poles is not yet fully understood.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A phase-type distribution is the distribution of the absorption time of a continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space {1,...,n,n+1}, where state n+1 is absorbing and states 1,...,n are transient. Such a distribution is specified by a pair (α, A), called a phase-type representation, where α is a row sub-stochastic probability vector on {1,...,n} (the initial distribution on the transient states) and A is an n×n subgenerator matrix (off-diagonal entries nonnegative, row sums ≤ 0, and A nonsingular). The density is f(t) = α e^{At}(-A)·1 for t ≥ 0, and the Laplace transform is α(sI − A)^{-1}(-A)·1, a rational function whose poles are eigenvalues of A.

To a representation (α, A) one associates its directed graph G(α,A) on vertices {1,...,n,n+1}, with an arc i → j (i ≠ j, i,j ∈ {1,...,n}) whenever A_{ij} > 0, and an arc i → n+1 whenever (-A·1)_i > 0. The representation is called acyclic if G(α,A) has no directed cycle among the transient states, and cyclic otherwise. The order of a representation is its number n of transient states; the order of a phase-type distribution F is the minimum order over all representations of F.

Investigate the following questions:

(a) Characterize precisely the phase-type distributions F for which every phase-type representation is cyclic (i.e., cyclicity is compulsory). In particular, prove or disprove: a phase-type distribution F admits an acyclic representation if and only if the Laplace transform of F has only real poles.

(b) Suppose F has only real poles (so an acyclic representation exists). Determine when F nevertheless admits a "natural" cyclic representation of order no larger than (or strictly smaller than) the minimum acyclic order, and give a constructive characterization of such cases.

(c) Decide whether there exists a phase-type distribution F all of whose cyclic representations have strictly smaller order than every acyclic representation of F, and characterize the class of such distributions.
artifact.status_search_result: The relationship between cyclicity of a phase-type representation and non-real poles of the Laplace transform is acknowledged as not fully understood in the literature. It is known that if the Laplace transform has only real poles, an acyclic representation exists; the monocyclic / bidiagonal representations of Mocanu–Commault provide canonical cyclic forms. However, a complete characterization of when cyclicity is compulsory, when cyclic representations beat acyclic ones in order, and the general minimal-order question remain open problems.

status_evidence.title: The Order of Phase-Type Distributions
status_evidence.snippet: Result on order in terms of denominator/numerator degree cannot be extended to numerator degree two nor to non-real poles.
status_evidence.claim: The minimal-order question for phase-type distributions with non-real poles is not fully resolved.

status_evidence.title: On the canonical representation of phase type distributions
status_evidence.snippet: Monocyclic / bidiagonal canonical representations introduced to handle complex poles via cyclic structures.
status_evidence.claim: Cyclic canonical forms are used to represent distributions with non-real poles.

status_evidence.title: Phase-type distributions and representations: Some results
status_evidence.snippet: The relation between the cyclicity of the representation and the existence of non-real poles is not yet fully understood.
status_evidence.claim: The cyclicity vs non-real poles question is stated as open.
